I have a loop over a large array of small integers that adds up every value above a threshold. When I sort the array before the loop, the loop itself runs about six times faster, even though it does exactly the same number of additions and comparisons either way.

for (unsigned i = 0; i < n; ++i)
    if (data[i] >= 128) sum += data[i];

I expected the sort to make no difference at all, since every element is still visited once. Is this something about the cache, or about the compiler, or something else entirely that I am not seeing?

    It is worth saying for anyone who finds this later that the effect depends heavily on the compiler and the flags. At higher optimisation levels several compilers turn this particular branch into a conditional move or even vectorise the whole loop, and then the sorted and unsorted runs take exactly the same time. So if you cannot reproduce it, check the generated code before you check anything else, because the difference is in the instructions the compiler chose.

You are a victim of branch prediction failure.

A modern processor does not wait to find out which way a branch goes. It guesses, starts working on the guessed path, and throws that work away if the guess turns out to be wrong, which costs it a dozen or more cycles each time.

With sorted data the guess is almost always right: the branch goes one way for the first half of the array and the other way for the second, and the predictor learns that within a few iterations.

T = branch taken
N = branch not taken

data[] = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ... 126, 127, 128, 129, 130, ... 250, 251, 252, ...
branch = N  N  N  N  N  ...   N    N    T    T    T  ...   T    T    T  ...

With random data the branch is taken about half the time with no pattern at all, so the predictor is wrong about half the time and every wrong guess throws work away. That is the whole of the six times: the same instructions, but a great many of them started and then discarded. If you remove the branch, for example by computing a mask from the comparison and adding the masked value unconditionally, the sorted and unsorted versions run at the same speed, and on most machines both run faster than either did before.

Iver Sandqvist Jul 12, 2020
The railway analogy in the older version of this answer helped me more than any textbook did, but it hides one thing that matters in practice: a mispredicted branch does not only cost the cycles thrown away, it also stops the processor from doing anything useful further ahead while it recovers. That is why the penalty is so much larger on long pipelines, and why it keeps growing as processors get wider and their pipelines deeper.
